_comment: Critical voter-service facts. Only a human editor changes this file, with CODEOWNER review. CI fails if data.js differs from these values.

values.dates[0].pastNote: Closed for this election. You can still check your status.
values.dates[1].s: Your mailed application must arrive by this date
values.dates[2].s: Last day to hand in a regular application at your county’s absentee office. Emergency applications have later deadlines.
values.dates[3].s: By hand: before your county office closes, 5 p.m. at the latest. By mail: it must arrive by noon Nov 3.
values.dates[3].pastNote: Hand delivery has closed. A mailed ballot counts only if it arrives by noon Nov 3.
values.absenteeStages[0].title: Can’t make it to the polls on Nov. 3?
values.absenteeStages[0].text: You may qualify to vote absentee if you’ll be out of your county (including at college), work a required shift of 10 hours or more during polling hours, are ill or disabled, or care for a homebound family member. Don’t count on the mail now: a mailed application must arrive by Tue, Oct. 27. Apply in person at your county’s absentee office by Thu, Oct. 29 instead.
values.absenteeStages[1].title: Need an absentee ballot?
values.absenteeStages[1].text: The mail deadline has passed. If you qualify, you can still apply in person at your county’s absentee office through Thu, Oct. 29. Already have a ballot? Return it by hand before your county’s absentee office closes Mon, Nov. 2 (5 p.m. at the latest), or by mail so it arrives by noon Nov. 3.
values.absenteeStages[2].title: Voting on Tuesday, Nov. 3
values.absenteeStages[2].text: Regular absentee applications are closed. Already have a ballot? Return it by hand before your county’s absentee office closes Mon, Nov. 2 (5 p.m. at the latest), or by mail so it arrives by noon Nov. 3. An emergency in the last five days, such as a medical emergency, an unexpected work requirement or a death in the family, may still qualify you for an emergency absentee ballot. Ask your county’s absentee election manager right away: the application is due by 5 p.m. Mon, Nov. 2 (noon Nov. 3 for your own medical emergency), and unless it’s a medical emergency, you must bring it in yourself. Otherwise, vote at your polling place on Tuesday, Nov. 3, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
values.absenteeStages[3].title: Voted a provisional ballot?
values.absenteeStages[3].text: If you voted a provisional ballot because you didn’t have a photo ID, bring a valid photo ID to your county Board of Registrars by 5 p.m. Friday, Nov. 6, so your vote can be counted.

vote[0].p: The deadline to register for this election was Monday, Oct. 19. Look up your registration, district, polling place, and sample ballot.

vote[1].p: Tuesday, Nov. 3, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. If you’re in line by 7 p.m., you can vote.
list: Alabama has no early voting. Voting before Election Day means voting absentee, which requires a qualifying reason.
On the ballot you can either vote a straight-party ticket or mark candidates one by one.
Some polling places near the Georgia line may run on Eastern Time (7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern). Check with your county if unsure.
Moved within your county since you registered? Go to the polling place for your new address, update your registration there, and vote a provisional ballot.
Moved to a different county? Your registration doesn’t move with you, and you can’t vote at your old polling place. Call the Board of Registrars in the county where you live now, before Election Day.
Not on the poll list, or poll workers can’t confirm your registration? Ask for a provisional ballot. It counts once officials confirm you’re eligible.
Asked for an absentee ballot but it never came, or you didn’t send it back? You can vote a provisional ballot at your polling place.
Alabama driver’s license or nondriver ID
Free Alabama Photo Voter ID card, available from your county Board of Registrars, even on Election Day
U.S. passport, military ID, or tribal ID
Other photo ID issued by Alabama, another state or the federal government, such as a pistol permit or a Department of Corrections release ID
Employee photo ID from the federal government or from an Alabama state, county or city government
Student or employee ID from an Alabama college, or from a public college in another state
vote[2].after: Bring the physical card. Under a 2026 state law (HB110, in effect since Oct. 1), digital IDs, including Alabama’s digital driver’s license, aren’t accepted for voting, even though some older Secretary of State guides, including the 2026 Voter Guide PDF, still list it. A driver’s license or nondriver ID expired less than 60 days still counts. Licenses or IDs issued to foreign nationals can’t be used for voting.

vote[3].p: Applications for the Nov. 3 election are closed: the deadlines were Tue, Oct 27 by mail and Thu, Oct 29 in person. Absentee voting requires a qualifying reason; the most common:
list: You’ll be out of your county on Election Day, including at college or in the military
You have a required work shift of 10 hours or more that overlaps polling hours
You’re ill or have a disability that keeps you from the polls
You’re caring for a family member who is confined at home
You’re a poll worker at a polling place other than your own

deadlines.caption: Absentee deadlines for Nov. 3

rows.h: By hand (at your county’s absentee office)
c: Mon, Nov 2, before the office closes (5 p.m. at the latest)

deadlines.note: Both application deadlines have passed. If you already have your ballot, a mailed ballot can still arrive as late as noon Tue, Nov 3.

ol: Already have your ballot? Mark it and sign the affidavit in front of a notary or two witnesses age 18 or older. Without this, your ballot can’t be counted. Online or remote notarization isn’t allowed.

Return the ballot yourself: by hand before your county’s absentee office closes on Mon, Nov 2 (5 p.m. at the latest), or by mail or a carrier such as FedEx or UPS so it arrives by noon Tue, Nov 3. Except in a medical emergency, no one else may return it for you.
vote[3].after: Voting from the military or overseas? See “Military and overseas voters” below.

vote[4].p: You may still get an emergency absentee ballot if one of these happens within five days of the election and you didn’t know about it before the regular deadline:
list: Your employer unexpectedly requires you to be away from your polling place while the polls are open
You need emergency treatment from a doctor
You’re caring for someone who needs emergency treatment from a doctor
A close relative dies, such as a parent, child, sibling, grandparent or grandchild (including in-laws)
vote[4].after: Contact your county’s absentee election manager right away. Take the application to the office yourself, with a copy of your photo ID; only a medical-emergency application can be mailed, sent by carrier, or brought by someone else. Apply by 5 p.m. Mon, Nov 2. After you vote, hand the ballot to the absentee election manager yourself by noon Tue, Nov 3; it can’t be mailed or returned by someone else. For your own medical emergency, your doctor certifies it, you can apply as late as noon Tue, Nov 3, and someone you choose can turn in your application, pick up your ballot and return it.

Absentee election manager guide (Secretary of State, PDF)

vote[5].p: Service members, their spouses and dependents, and U.S. citizens living overseas vote absentee under a federal law (UOCAVA), with a few differences:
list: Apply by the same dates as other absentee voters. You can ask to get your ballot by email.
Your ballot counts if it’s postmarked by Tue, Nov 3, and arrives by noon Tue, Nov 10.
Outside the U.S. and got your ballot by email? You can return it electronically until 11:59 p.m. on Election Day, Tue, Nov 3; instructions come with the ballot.
You don’t need to include a copy of a photo ID.
Ballot hasn’t arrived? Use the Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB) as a backup. The same postmark and arrival deadlines apply.

Military and overseas voting (Secretary of State)

vote[6].p: If two election officials at your polling place positively identify you as a voter on the poll list and sign a sworn statement, you can vote a regular ballot. Otherwise, you can vote a provisional ballot, which counts once officials confirm you’re eligible; to have it counted, bring a valid photo ID to your county Board of Registrars by 5 p.m. Friday, Nov. 6.

vote[7].p: Call the Secretary of State’s Elections Division at 334‑242‑7210 (toll-free 1‑800‑274‑8683), or your county Board of Registrars.

callout.title: Can’t make it to the polls on Nov. 3?
callout.text: You may be able to vote absentee if you’ll be out of your county (including away at college), work a required shift of 10 hours or more during polling hours, are ill or disabled, or care for a homebound family member. Mailed applications must arrive by Tuesday, Oct. 27, and the ballot needs a notary or two witnesses.

idCard.title: Bring a photo ID
idCard.text: A physical photo ID, such as a driver’s license or a free Alabama Photo Voter ID. No ID? If two election officials positively identify you and sign a sworn statement, you can vote a regular ballot. Otherwise you can vote a provisional ballot and show ID by 5 p.m. Fri, Nov. 6.

spanish.text: ¿Prefiere español? Información para votar en Alabama:

spanishGuide.title: Lo esencial en español
spanishGuide.intro: Las fechas y reglas para votar el 3 de noviembre de 2026 en Alabama. Las descripciones de los candidatos están solo en inglés.

items.p: Martes 3 de noviembre, de 7 a.m. a 7 p.m. Si está en la fila a las 7 p.m., puede votar. Alabama no tiene votación anticipada: para votar antes, hay que votar en ausencia, con un motivo válido.
El plazo para inscribirse para esta elección venció el lunes 19 de octubre. Verifique su inscripción, su lugar de votación y su boleta de muestra en el sitio oficial del estado (en inglés).

Lleve una identificación física con foto, como una licencia de conducir de Alabama, la identificación de votante con foto de Alabama (gratuita) o un pasaporte de EE. UU. No se aceptan identificaciones digitales. Si no tiene identificación, puede votar con una boleta provisional y presentar una identificación ante la Junta de Registradores de su condado antes de las 5 p.m. del viernes 6 de noviembre.

Necesita un motivo que lo califique, por ejemplo, estar fuera de su condado el día de las elecciones o tener una enfermedad o discapacidad. El plazo para solicitar la boleta ya venció: la solicitud debía llegar por correo a más tardar el martes 27 de octubre o entregarse en persona a más tardar el jueves 29 de octubre. Si ya tiene su boleta, la boleta completada se entrega en mano antes de que cierre la oficina el lunes 2 de noviembre (a más tardar a las 5 p.m.), o por correo, y debe llegar antes del mediodía del martes 3 de noviembre. Las boletas de votantes militares y en el extranjero cuentan si tienen matasellos a más tardar del 3 de noviembre y llegan antes del mediodía del martes 10 de noviembre. Si están fuera del país y recibieron la boleta por correo electrónico, pueden devolverla por vía electrónica hasta las 11:59 p.m. del martes 3 de noviembre.

Si en los cinco días antes de la elección tiene una emergencia que no conocía antes del plazo normal (una obligación de trabajo imprevista, una emergencia médica suya o de alguien a quien cuida, o la muerte de un familiar cercano), puede calificar para una boleta de voto en ausencia de emergencia. Consulte de inmediato en la oficina de voto en ausencia de su condado. Lleve la solicitud usted mismo, con una copia de su identificación con foto; solo una solicitud por emergencia médica puede enviarse por correo o por servicio de mensajería, o entregarla otra persona. Preséntela a más tardar a las 5 p.m. del lunes 2 de noviembre y, después de votar, entregue usted mismo la boleta en la oficina de voto en ausencia antes del mediodía del martes 3 de noviembre; no puede enviarse por correo ni entregarla otra persona. Si la emergencia médica es suya, su médico la certifica, puede presentar la solicitud hasta el mediodía del martes 3 de noviembre y una persona de su elección puede entregar la solicitud, recoger la boleta y devolverla.
Llame a la División Electoral de la Secretaría de Estado al 334‑242‑7210 o, sin costo, al 1‑800‑274‑8683.
